claims.claim: Amino acids are molecules that combine to form proteins; amino acids and proteins are described as the building blocks of life.
The human body commonly builds proteins from about 20 amino acids; OpenStax's nutrition textbook lists exactly 20 (9 essential + 11 nonessential) and Harvard describes twenty-plus building blocks.

The 9 essential amino acids for adults are histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and valine; essential means the body cannot make them, so they must come from food.

Nonessential amino acids (alanine, arginine, asparagine, aspartic acid, cysteine, glutamic acid, glutamine, glycine, proline, serine, tyrosine) can be produced by the body even if they are not eaten; a smaller group is conditionally essential, needed from food in times of illness and stress.

The body uses amino acids to make proteins that help break down food, grow, and repair body tissue, and it can use amino acids as an energy source; proteins include enzymes that power chemical reactions and hormones that carry signals.
When proteins are digested or broken down, amino acids are the result; digestion breaks dietary protein into individual amino acids that the body reassembles into the proteins it needs.

Amino acids are found in animal sources (meats, milk, fish, eggs) and in plant sources (soy, beans, legumes, nut butters, and some grains such as quinoa); people do not need to eat animal products to get all the amino acids they need.

A diet based on a single plant item is not adequate, but pairing complementary proteins at a single meal (such as beans with rice) is no longer the focus; the balance of amino acids over the whole day is what matters, and a variety of plant foods each day supplies all the amino acids needed.
The body does not stockpile amino acids like fat; it keeps a working pool, and excess amino acids are converted to glucose or triglycerides for energy or stripped of nitrogen and excreted.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The old 'combine plant proteins at every meal' rule (beans with rice, corn with beans) vs modern guidance.
positions: Older nutrition guidance held that complementary plant foods had to be eaten at the same meal to provide complete protein.

Current guidance (MedlinePlus, Harvard Nutrition Source) holds that pairing at a single meal is unnecessary; the balance of amino acids over the whole day is what matters, and a variety of plant foods across the day supplies the essential amino acids.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the modern position: variety across the day, with complete plant proteins (soy, quinoa, chia seeds) noted as options. The older every-meal rule is presented as historical context, not current guidance.

sourceRecords.title: The Nutrition Source: Protein
sourceRecords.provider: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A/B (top academic institution). Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: protein is found throughout the body and makes up the enzymes that power chemical reactions and the hemoglobin that carries oxygen; at least 10,000 different proteins; protein is made from twenty-plus basic building blocks called amino acids; the body does not store amino acids and makes them from scratch or by modifying others; nine essential amino acids (named) must come from food; complete proteins contain all needed amino acids while incomplete proteins lack one or more of the nine essential; animal foods tend to be complete while plant foods often lack one or more; people who eat no animal foods can eat a variety of protein-containing plant foods each day to get all amino acids, and can choose complete plant proteins like quinoa and chia seeds.
